prompt.context: Our client, Dopamine, is the fourth largest manufacturer of drugs internationally. Two years ago, Dopamine invented a drug – tentatively branded Soma – to treat acute depression. Unlike most antidepressants, the drug is preventative rather than responsive. Whereas most antidepressants attempt to treat diagnosed cases of depression, Soma is designed for consumption before symptoms emerge. It is aimed at individuals who are deemed 'high-risk' for acute depression due to family history, an acute trauma, or a variety of other factors. The drug is available by prescription only and it has no known side effects. Soma received regulatory approval by the FDA, and Dopamine is considering how to price the drug in the United States.
prompt.question: You have been asked to size the market and recommend a price for Soma.

clarifying_info.q: Has the drug been covered by insurance yet?
clarifying_info.a: The drug has not yet been covered by insurance.

clarifying_info.q: What are the medical costs for acute depression?
clarifying_info.a: Medical bills for acute depression average $10,000 annually per case (i.e. per patient). This includes costs associated with drugs, therapy, and hospitalization.

clarifying_info.q: What were the development costs for Soma?

clarifying_info.a: The drug is a single tablet taken on a daily basis.

framework: Market sizing: estimate the number of high-risk individuals in the US and the total market size in dollars
Competitor/substitute analysis: assess existing antidepressants and their pricing; consider lack of direct substitutes for a preventative drug
Product analysis: strengths (preventative, no side effects, FDA approved, unique mechanism), weaknesses (not yet covered by insurance, radically new concept requiring physician/patient adoption)
Pricing model: compare value-based pricing (savings to insurers vs. treating acute depression) vs. cost-based pricing (variable cost + margin)
Insurance coverage: determine whether insurers will cover Soma at a given price by comparing total costs under current treatment model vs. new drug model

questions.prompt: What factors do you think are most critical to the price of the drug?
questions.guidance: Strong answers should brainstorm across multiple dimensions: uniqueness and lack of substitutes; public and physician acceptance of a preventative mental-health drug; regulatory and reimbursement environment; and critically, whether insurers will cover the drug. Insurance coverage is the pivotal factor — without it, the drug will not gain market traction. Other relevant factors: effectiveness, safety profile, competitive landscape, development cost recovery expectations.

questions.prompt: How would the insurance company decide whether to cover the drug?
questions.guidance: The decision is fundamentally a cost comparison: is the total cost to insurers under the current treatment model higher or lower than the total cost under a treatment model that includes Soma? If Soma reduces net insurer costs (or at least does not raise them materially), insurers have a financial incentive to cover it.

questions.prompt: A price of $50 per package (10 pills) has been floated. Would an insurer cover Soma at this price? Use the following assumptions: 300M people in the US; 1 in 200 Americans suffer from acute depression per year; 1 in 100 Americans are considered at risk, and of that group 1 in 5 are high-risk (assume all high-risk individuals would develop acute depression without the drug); Soma is 70% effective (30% still develop depression and also incur $10,000 in treatment costs on top of Soma costs); all individuals with acute depression receive treatment; annual treatment for acute depression costs $10,000 per case.
questions.guidance: Candidate must compute total insurer costs under the current model vs. the new-drug model and compare them.

math.setup: Compare Current Cost vs. New Drug Cost. Current cost = (US population × incidence rate) × cost per case. New drug cost = cost of Soma for all high-risk individuals + cost of treating Soma failures + cost of treating unidentified cases.
steps: Soma cost for high-risk: 600,000 × $50/package ÷ 10 pills × 365 days = 600,000 × $1,825 ≈ $1.095B ≈ ~$1B
Cost of Soma failures (30% who still develop depression): 600,000 × 0.30 × $10,000 = $1.8B
Unidentified cases not reached by Soma: 1.5M total cases − 600,000 high-risk = 900,000; 900,000 × $10,000 = $9B
Comparison: Current $15B > New ~$12B → insurers save ~$3B; they would likely cover the drug at $50/package
math.answer: Total new drug costs (~$12B) are less than current treatment costs ($15B), so insurers would likely cover Soma at $50 per package.

questions.prompt: What would you charge for the drug? Could you charge more than $50?
questions.guidance: No calculation required. Strong answer: insurers would accept any price that keeps new drug total costs at or below the current $15B. There is upward pricing room — the breakeven price for insurers is higher than $50. However, adoption dynamics (physician acceptance, patient willingness, new concept risk) may argue for a more conservative launch price. Candidates should note the trade-off between maximizing price and ensuring adoption.

questions.prompt: What single factor would allow Dopamine to raise prices substantially?
questions.guidance: Improved screening. Currently only 1 in 500 Americans (600,000 out of 300M) are identified as high-risk, while 1 in 200 (1.5M) actually develop acute depression. Better screening tools that identify a larger proportion of the at-risk population would expand the addressable market and increase Soma's total value to insurers, supporting a higher price.

questions.prompt: The client believes the $500M development cost must be covered by future revenues or the company should not proceed with production. Is this correct?
questions.guidance: No. The $500M development cost is a sunk cost — it has already been spent and is irrelevant to the forward-looking production decision. What matters is whether future revenues cover variable (and fixed) costs of production going forward.

questions.prompt: Variable costs of production are $10 per package of 10 pills. Fixed costs are zero. What is the margin and markup at a price of $50?
Indulge the client: assuming the $500M development cost must be recovered, what is the breakeven period? Assume a negligible discount rate.
questions.guidance: Use annual profit from the 600,000 high-risk individuals who take Soma.

math.setup: Annual profit per package = Price − Variable cost = $50 − $10 = $40. All 600,000 high-risk individuals take one pill per day (365 days, 10 pills per package → 36.5 packages/year ≈ 36.5 packages).
steps: Breakeven = $500M / $876M ≈ 0.57 years ≈ 6–7 months (casebook rounds to ~7–8 months using $0.8B)
math.answer: Breakeven period is approximately 7–8 months (roughly 0.6 years).

brainstorming.prompt: What factors are most critical to the price of Soma?

categories.name: Market & competitive dynamics
ideas: Lack of direct substitutes (first-of-kind preventative antidepressant)
Competitive landscape of existing responsive antidepressants
Potential future entrants once patent expires

categories.name: Insurer & payer considerations
ideas: Whether insurers will cover the drug (pivotal factor for market traction)
Cost savings to insurers vs. current treatment model
Negotiating leverage of large pharmacy benefit managers

categories.name: Adoption & acceptance
ideas: Public and physician acceptance of a radically new preventative mental-health concept
Patient willingness to take a daily pill without current symptoms
Prescribing behavior and clinical guideline adoption

categories.name: Product characteristics
ideas: No known side effects — reduces adoption friction
Requires accurate screening/identification of high-risk individuals

categories.name: Pricing strategy
ideas: Value-based ceiling: price that keeps insurer costs at or below current treatment costs
Cost-based floor: variable production cost of $10/package
Penetration vs. premium pricing trade-off for initial launch

recommendation: Dopamine should launch Soma in the United States at a price in the range of $50 per package (10 pills), or potentially higher up to the level at which insurer net costs equal current treatment costs (~$15B)
At $50/package, total insurer costs under the new model (~$12B) are well below the current $15B baseline, giving insurers a strong financial incentive to add Soma to their formularies
The addressable market is approximately 600,000 high-risk individuals; at $50/package the drug generates ~$0.9B in annual profit and recovers its $500M development cost in under one year
risks: Insurer adoption may lag despite favorable economics if internal approval processes are slow or if insurers require real-world efficacy data
Physician and patient acceptance of a preventative paradigm for mental health is uncertain and may limit actual uptake below the theoretical 600,000 high-risk population
Improved screening (only 1/500 Americans currently identified vs. 1/200 who develop the disease) limits both market reach and pricing power
If the drug is not covered by insurance, out-of-pocket cost at $50/package × 365 days = ~$1,825/year is likely prohibitive for most patients
next_steps: Engage major insurers early to model cost savings and negotiate formulary inclusion
Invest in improving screening tools and clinical criteria to identify more high-risk individuals, expanding the addressable market
Conduct physician education campaigns to drive prescribing of a preventative mental-health drug
Monitor 30% failure cohort closely and assess whether a tiered pricing or combination therapy model could further reduce insurer costs
